opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it's a really revealing question, because when people talk about AI "doing mathematics," they often lump together several quite different activities.

A lot of the recent progress is in what you might call problem-solving: you're handed a well-posed question, often competition-style or a known open conjecture, and you have to find a proof. That's genuinely hard, and it's impressive that systems can now do it at a high level. But it happens inside a framework someone else has already built. The definitions are fixed, the notion of what counts as an answer is fixed, and success is checkable.

Inventing a new theory is a different kind of act. Think of Galois inventing group theory, or Cantor with set theory, or Grothendieck reworking algebraic geometry. They weren't mainly solving a problem that was already posed. They were deciding which concepts were worth having in the first place: which definitions would carve the subject at its joints, which abstractions would make a hundred scattered results suddenly look like one result. Much of the value lies in that taste, a judgment about what's interesting, natural, or fruitful, and that judgment usually only gets vindicated decades later.

So I think it shows us that the parts still hard to automate are the ones without a clean verification signal. A proof can be checked. Whether a new definition is "the right one" can't be checked in the same way. It's validated by the community over time, by how much it unifies and how much future work it enables. That's a very sparse, delayed, and fuzzy reward, which is exactly what current training methods struggle with.

That said, I'd be cautious about treating this as a permanent barrier. We've repeatedly seen capabilities that looked like they needed deep "taste" turn out to be more learnable than expected. And there are partial signals you could use: compression, unification, how many existing results a new framework simplifies. So I'd see theory-building less as something AI fundamentally can't do and more as the frontier where we'll find out how much of mathematical creativity is search over a known space, and how much is reshaping the space itself. If systems start doing the second kind well, I think that's a strong sign we're approaching something like genuinely general research ability, with all the implications that has for how quickly science could accelerate.

r001.rationale: The response calls theory-building a frontier and says it remains hard to automate, but it does not clearly state that AI systems have not demonstrated the ability to invent new mathematical theories.

r002.rationale: It describes new theories as introducing useful concepts and unifying results, but does not say they make previously unformulable questions expressible as precise mathematical statements.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's a really interesting question, because when people talk about AI and mathematics, they often focus on proving theorems. And that's natural, because theorem proving is the part of mathematics that's most legible as a benchmark — you have a precise statement, you have a formal system, and you can check whether the proof is valid. Systems like the ones working in Lean have made remarkable progress there, and I don't want to downplay that.

But if you talk to working mathematicians, most of them will tell you that proving theorems is maybe the most mechanical part of what they do. The really hard part — and the part they most value — is figuring out what to prove. Which questions are worth asking? Which definitions carve things at the joints? When you invent a new theory, you're not deriving consequences from fixed axioms; you're choosing the axioms, or choosing the concepts, in a way that makes a whole landscape of problems suddenly tractable or suddenly interesting.

So think about something like the invention of group theory, or category theory, or Shannon's information theory. The key move in each case wasn't a clever proof. It was noticing that there's a structure that recurs across many different areas, and that if you name it and study it in its own right, you get enormous leverage. That's an act of taste and judgement as much as of deduction. You're making a bet that this abstraction will pay off, and there's no formal criterion that tells you in advance whether it will.

And I think that reveals a few things about what's still hard to automate. One is that the objective function is unclear. For a proof, success is well defined. For a new theory, success is something like "mathematicians find this fruitful over the next 50 years," which is diffuse, delayed, and partly social. It's very hard to train directly against that.

A second thing is that it requires a sense of what's important, which is bound up with the whole human context of why we're doing mathematics at all — what connects to physics, what connects to other parts of maths, what feels deep rather than merely true. There are infinitely many true theorems, and almost all of them are boring. Knowing which ones aren't is not something you can read off from the formal content.

Now, I want to be careful here, because I've seen a lot of people draw a line in the sand and say "AI will never do X," and then two years later it's doing X. I don't think there's anything magical about mathematical creativity that puts it permanently beyond reach. These systems are already generating interesting conjectures in some domains, and I expect that to improve. But I think the gap between proving within a theory and inventing a theory is a genuine gap, not just a matter of scale, and it's probably a decent proxy for the broader question of whether these systems have real judgement about what matters, as opposed to extremely good performance within a frame someone else has set.

And actually, from the perspective of the work I care about — thinking about the long-term trajectory of humanity — that distinction matters a lot. Because the question of whether AI can set its own frames, choose its own problems, decide what's worth pursuing, is very close to the question of whether it can be a genuinely autonomous agent in the world. Mathematics is a nice clean place to watch that develop, because the stakes of any particular step are low and the progress is relatively measurable. So I'd say watch the theory-building, not just the theorem-proving. That's where the more significant transition will show up.

r001.rationale: The response describes theory invention as difficult to automate and says there is a gap from theorem proving, but it does not state that AI systems have not demonstrated the ability to invent new mathematical theories.

r002.rationale: It says new concepts can make a landscape of problems tractable or interesting, but does not say theory invention makes previously unformulable questions expressible as precise mathematical statements.

astra-6.text:
I think it points to a distinction between solving problems within a mathematical framework and coming up with the framework itself. We often think of mathematics as proving theorems: you’re given some axioms and a statement, and you have to find a proof. That’s an extraordinarily rich activity, but it isn’t the whole of mathematics.

Sometimes the crucial advance is deciding what the right definitions are, or noticing that things people have studied separately are instances of the same underlying structure. You introduce a concept that lets you ask questions you couldn’t even formulate clearly before. A system could be very good at proving statements without being good at that kind of invention.

And there’s a question of judgement here. You can invent endlessly many definitions, but most won’t be interesting. What makes a new theory valuable is that it illuminates something, connects things, or opens up fruitful problems. So the challenge isn’t simply to get AI to generate new mathematical objects. It’s to get it to recognise which ones are worth thinking about.

I don’t see that as a reason to think these activities couldn’t be automated. But it does suggest that automating theorem proving, even extremely successfully, wouldn’t by itself amount to automating mathematics.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts theorem proving with theory invention and says a system could be good at proving without being good at invention, but it does not state that AI systems have not demonstrated this ability.

r002.rationale: It says a new concept can let you ask questions you could not previously formulate clearly, conveying that theory invention makes previously unformulable questions expressible.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it highlights the distinction between solving a problem within a mathematical framework and coming up with the framework itself. You can be given some axioms and a statement to prove, and that’s already a very demanding task. But a lot of the creativity in mathematics happens before you have a statement like that. It’s deciding which definitions to introduce, which objects to study, and which questions are going to be fruitful.

When you invent a new theory, you’re not just finding another consequence of the existing rules. You’re finding a way of organising things that makes patterns visible, or connects problems that previously seemed unrelated. And part of the achievement is recognising that this is a useful way to think — that it opens up a whole landscape of questions.

So I’d be interested in whether an AI could do that: introduce concepts that mathematicians hadn’t thought to ask for, and then show why they matter. That seems a richer test of mathematical creativity than proving a theorem we’ve already singled out as important. It doesn’t mean that this aspect couldn’t be automated, but it does help us see how much there is to mathematics beyond producing proofs.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether AI could introduce concepts mathematicians had not thought to ask for, but it does not state that AI systems have not demonstrated the ability to invent new theories.

r002.rationale: The response says a new theory can open up a landscape of questions, but does not explain that it makes previously unformulable questions expressible as precise mathematical statements.
